title: What is Collectors.teeing(downstream1, downstream2, merger) (Java 12+): running TWO collectors in a single pass and merging their results: e.g. computing min AND max salary simultaneously: and why is it more efficient than streaming twice?
shortTitle: Collectors.teeing: two collectors in one pass, merge results (Java 12+)
keyPoints: Collectors.teeing runs two collectors simultaneously on the same stream in a single pass
Each element is fed to BOTH downstream collectors independently
The merger BiFunction combines both results into one final value when the stream is exhausted
More efficient than two separate streams because data is iterated only once
Named after a plumbing T-joint: one input splits into two outputs, then merged
Java 12+ (JEP not numbered, added as API enhancement)
Works with any two collectors: minBy+maxBy, counting+summing, filtering+grouping

s1_definition.oneliner: Collectors.teeing runs two collectors on the same stream in one pass and merges their results with a BiFunction, computing two aggregates simultaneously.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Signature** – `teeing(Collector<T,?,R1> downstream1, Collector<T,?,R2> downstream2, BiFunction<R1,R2,R> merger)`.
- **Behavior** – every stream element is fed to BOTH downstream collectors. When the stream ends, the merger combines both results.
- **Efficiency** – one iteration instead of two; important for large datasets or I/O-backed streams.
- **Naming** – named after a plumbing T-joint: one input pipe splits into two outputs, then the outputs are joined.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh needs both the smallest and largest transaction from his bank statement. Without teeing, the bank scans all 1000 transactions once for the smallest, then scans again for the largest. With teeing, one scanner reads each transaction and simultaneously updates two trackers (min and max). At the end, both results are available. Half the work.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Collectors.teeing runs two collectors on the same stream in a single pass and merges their results with a BiFunction. Each element is fed to both downstream collectors simultaneously. The merger combines both results into one final value when the stream is exhausted.

This is more efficient than creating separate streams: for min+max, teeing makes one pass instead of two. For count+sum, one pass instead of two. For nested teeing with four metrics (min, max, count, sum), one pass instead of four.

In a banking analytics service, computing the salary range (min and max) with `teeing(minBy, maxBy, SalaryRange::new)` produces both extremes in a single iteration. The merger can be a record constructor for the cleanest code. For empty streams, both downstream collectors return their identity values and the merger handles them.

Remember one sentence: Collectors.teeing runs two collectors in one pass and merges their results, computing multiple aggregates simultaneously instead of iterating twice.
